curriculum: CC K.CC.A.1 count to 100 by ones and tens; K.CC.A.2 count on from any number; K.CC.A.3 write numerals 0-20 and match to sets, 0 for empty set; K.CC.B.4 (a) one word per object and one object per word, (b) last word gives total, total is independent of arrangement or order, (c) each next number is one more; K.CC.B.5 count up to 20 in line/array/circle and 10 scattered, count out a given number [ccKCC, opened]. Brief codes K.CC.A.1-3 and B.4-5 are correct.
CC 1.NBT.A.1 count to 120 from any start below 120, read/write numerals; 2.NBT.A.2 count to 1000, skip-count by 5s, 10s, 100s [cc1NBT, cc2NBT, opened]. Add to brief.

England PoS Y1: count forwards/backwards to and across 100 from 0, 1 or any number; count, read, write numerals to 100; count in 2s, 5s, 10s; one more/one less; read/write 1-20 as numerals and words. Y2: count in 2s, 3s, 5s from 0, in 10s from any number, forwards and backwards; read/write to at least 100 in numerals and words [eng, opened]. Brief 'KS1 Y1-Y2 number and place value' is correct but Y3 (4, 8, 50, 100) and Y4 (6, 7, 9, 25, 1000, negatives) also count in steps.

Korean 2022 curriculum text NOT opened: the vivasam/koreascience PDFs returned binary data. Korean codes in brief.json are unverified and may be 2015 or 2022 codes; two 2015-curriculum codes were seen quoted in a paper: [2수01-01] understand numbers 0-100, count/read/write them; [2수01-02] understand 일/십/백/천 place values and positional notation, read/write up to four-digit numbers (source kor15).
textbooks: IM K Unit 1 (A tools, B Recognize Quantities up to 4 without counting, C Are There Enough?, D Counting Collections up to 10); Unit 2 A-C count objects and images, rearranging does not change count, 5-frames, circles, numerals; Unit 6 A Count 11-20 objects, C Count 11-20 images in lines, arrays, circles [imK, opened].

IM K U2 L1 'Fingers as a Math Tool': choral count to 10 with a finger per number, Math Fingers cards, show a numeral on fingers; teacher notes name verbal count sequence, one-to-one, subitizing, counting on from 5 [imK2L1, opened].

IM G1 U8 C Numbers to 120; G2 U5 A (three-digit numbers, counting 90-120 choral count in G2U5L1) [im1, im2U5L1, opened]. Brief 'IM G1 U4' is place value (two-digit numbers to 99), counting to 99 appears in G1U4L10 [im1U4L10, opened].
explanations: Fingers, one finger per word (IM K U2 L1).
Objects touched, pointed at, or moved from 'not counted' to 'counted' pile; lines, circles, scattered collections (Thompson on one-one principle; NCETM audit; CC K.CC.B.5).
Counting images on 5-frames, in circles, lines, arrays (IM K U2 B, U6 C).
Numeral cards matched to quantities; tower of cubes of n cubes (IM K2 L17).
Number path/track of numerals (IES toolkit calls it a 'number path').
Choral count: class chants a sequence and records it to see patterns, e.g. 90 to 120 (IM G2 U5 L1).
conventions: English counts 1-12 then teens 13-19 end in -teen (reversed order of ones and tens: 'fourteen' = four + ten); twenty-one reads tens-first. Teen/ty confusion (13 vs 30) is a known error [ncetmAudit]. (Statement about English forms is general knowledge, not from an opened page: unverified.)

Korean has two number-word sets: native (하나 둘 셋 ... 열, 스물) used for counting objects, people, ages with 살, and hours; Sino-Korean (일 이 삼 ... 십, 백) for dates, money, minutes, phone numbers and numbers above 99. Sino-Korean 11 = 십일 (ten-one), 21 = 이십일 (two-ten-one), so tens-ones order is regular. Native 11 = 열하나 [korNum, opened].
Korean groups big numbers by 10^4 (만, 억, 조); English by 10^3 (thousand, million) [korNum].
Common Core writes standards 'K.CC.A.1' etc.; England says 'Number - number and place value' [eng, ccKCC]. IM uses 'choral count' and 'counting collections' as routines [imK2L1].
misconceptions: Gelman & Gallistel (1978) five principles as summarised by Thompson: one-one, stable order, cardinal (how to count); abstraction, order-irrelevance (what can be counted). Errors: skipping/double-counting; a child who says 1,2,3 then 2,1,3 lacks stable order; recounting when asked 'how many' shows cardinality not secure; repeating the last word is not reliable evidence (Bermejo et al. 2004: many children who counted five objects starting from 'three' answered 'seven') [thompson, opened].

Staves: last-number-word error (treating 'five' as the name of the last object; asked to 'show me five' points to one object); reciting list with no link to quantity; counting on too early; cardinality matures last; hierarchical inclusion as a later big idea [staves, opened].
IES toolkit lists counting errors: coordination (words and objects mismatched), keeping-track, skimming (sweeping a finger without tagging each) [ies, opened].

NCETM audit: recounting a rearranged group instead of seeing the amount unchanged (conservation); grabbing too many when asked to 'get five'; counting back is harder; 13 vs 30 [ncetmAudit, opened]. Advice: line, circle, scattered arrangements; puppet that makes mistakes; count sounds/actions/unmovable things.
IM K U2 L1 note: mirrored hands can confuse a child copying a partner's fingers; students may think five is the most a hand can show [imK2L1].
tasks: Count a collection of up to 10 then 20 objects in different arrangements; say 'how many'; count out n objects from a pile (CC K.CC.B.5, IM K U1 D).
Count on from a given number; count back; count across decades (England Y1; CC K.CC.A.2).
Write the numeral for a set; draw a set for a numeral; 0 for none.
Choral counts by 1s, then 2s, 5s, 10s with pattern-spotting.
Facts later concepts need: counting gives 'one more' successor (K.CC.B.4c); last word = total; total independent of order (feeds comparing, composing, odd/even, sequences, measurement).

Brief codes correct.

England PoS Y1: use objects, pictures and a number line to show numbers with 'equal to, more than, less than (fewer), most, least'; Y2: compare and order numbers 0-100 using <, > and =; Y3: compare and order up to 1000; Y4: order and compare beyond 1000 [eng, opened]. KS3 and GCSE N1 not opened.

textbooks: IM K Unit 2 D 'Compare Numbers' (compare written numbers 1-10, one more/one less); NOT Unit 1 C as brief.json says (U1 C is 'Are There Enough?', matching one-to-one) [imK, opened]. Correct brief: 'IM K U2 D'.

IM K U2 L17 Order Towers and Numbers: build cube towers for a number, order towers or numerals, check by counting, notice each is one more than before; standards K.CC.B.4.c, K.CC.C.6, building to C.7 [imK2L17, opened].

IM G1 U4 C Compare Numbers to 99; L16 'Write Comparisons with Symbols': reading 49 > 45 and 45 < 49 as the same fact; game 'Greatest of Them All' placing digit cards in tens or ones; 'make the statement true' with a blank (e.g. blank < 35 has greatest value 34) [im1, im1U4L16, opened].
IM G2 U5 B Compare and Order Numbers within 1,000 using place value and number lines; G4 U4 C Compare, Order, Round within 1,000,000 [im2, im4, opened].

OpenStax Prealgebra 1.1: CORRECTION - the LibreTexts mirror says the section does not use <, > or = and conveys order only via the number line (larger to the right); the openstax.org summary mentions no comparison symbols either. Do not cite OS 1.1 for symbols [os11, osLT, opened].
explanations: Match one-to-one (lines between objects, pairing) and see which group has leftovers (CC K.CC.C.6; IM K U1 C).
Connecting-cube towers side by side, ordered smallest to largest (IM K2 L17).
Base-ten cubes: towers of ten and singles; compare tens first then ones (IM G1 U4 L16).
Number line: larger numbers further right (England Y1; OpenStax 1.1).
Place value digits left to right: compare the highest place first (CC 2.NBT.A.4, 4.NBT.A.2).
Words and symbols: 'greater than', 'less than', read statement aloud; symbol reversal 49 > 45 same as 45 < 49 (IM G1 L16).
conventions: Symbols < > = : England introduces words in Y1 and symbols in Y2; CC and IM introduce symbols in Grade 1 (two-digit) [eng, cc1NBT, im1U4L16]. England says 'fewer' is permitted alongside 'less' (hint of wording 'most, least') [eng]. Korean symbol/word conventions: unverified (not opened). Common US mnemonic of the 'alligator' is NOT from an opened source.
misconceptions: IM G1 L16 teacher note: if a child writes a false statement, ask them to read it aloud and then name other numbers that make it true [im1U4L16].
IM G1 U4 L10: digits keep own value by place (17 vs 71 vs 7 vs 70); attending to units not left-to-right [im1U4L10].
IM K2 L17: check by counting rather than by looking; a tower of 10 vs 6 [imK2L17].
Gervasoni 2011: many children can read, write and order 2/3-digit numbers but cannot interpret quantity; ordering success may overstate place-value understanding [gervasoni, opened].
IES toolkit: comparing and labeling magnitudes depends on increasing magnitude and successor principles; teach more/fewer/same with matching before numerals [ies, opened].
tasks: Which is more, fewer, same (two groups up to 10); compare numerals 1-10.
Order towers/numeral cards 1-10; one more, one less.
Compare two-digit numbers with symbols; fill blanks to make true; digit-card games.
Order three-digit numbers; place on a number line.
Facts later concepts need: ordering of whole numbers is total and leaves a successor chain; rightwards = greater on number line; compare high place first.

5-frames and 10-frames for parts of 5 and 10, teen numbers as full ten-frame plus ones (IM K U5, U6 B).
Pictures of groups and equations 5 = 2 + 3, 18 = 10 + 8 (CC K.OA.A.3, K.NBT.A.1).
Fingers, claps, role-play, spoken explanation (CC K.OA.A.1).
Part-part-whole model (NCETM spine 1.2); number bonds named in England Y1 (the picture of the bond is not shown on opened pages: unverified).

misconceptions: IM K U5 L1: the total stays the same however it is split; same number split different ways [imK5L1].
IES toolkit: comparing/combining small sets uses 5- and 10-frames and fingers; number combinations [ies, opened].
Staves: hierarchical inclusion (a number contains smaller ones) and compensation as later big ideas [staves, opened].
Specific misconception list for number bonds: not found on opened pages; unverified.

Number bond/part-part-whole diagram completing missing part.

K.NBT.A.1 (teens) is the entry point and is missing from brief.

England PoS Y2: recognise tens and ones value of each digit in a two-digit number; identify/represent/estimate numbers with different representations including number line; Y3 hundreds, tens, ones in three-digit numbers; Y4 place value in four-digit numbers, round to 10/100/1000, Roman numerals to C (Y4) [eng, opened]. NCETM spine: 1.8-1.10, 1.17-1.18, 1.22, 1.26, 1.30 progression of composition [ncetmSpine].

textbooks: IM G1 U4 'Numbers to 99': A Units of Ten (towers, drawings, number words), B Tens and Ones, C Compare, D Different Ways to Make a Number; L10 'Write Two-Digit Numbers' (cubes images 7, 70, 17, 71; '2 ones 8 tens'; 1-99 number path game; class judges '702 for seventy-two'); L5 Center Day 1 (groups of ten, base-ten diagram of 3 tens 5 ones, number 30) [im1, im1U4L10, im1U4L5, opened].

IM G2 U5 'Numbers to 1,000': A value of three digits; L1 'How Do We Compose a Hundred?': 8 tens 16 ones = 96; add ones to make 100; 100 ones = 10 tens = 1 hundred; fewest blocks; choral count 90-120 [im2, im2U5L1, opened].
IM G4 U4 B Place-value Relationships through 1,000,000: each place ten times the place to its right; G5 U5 A decimals to thousandths [im4, im5, opened].

OpenStax Prealgebra 1.1: counting vs whole numbers, number line, money model ($100/$10/$1 bills), base-10 blocks (cube, rod, flat), place-value chart in periods of three with commas, expanded form 100+30+8, naming rules (omit 'and', no 's' on period names), rounding by looking at digit to the right; Elementary Algebra 1.1 same text per search result only (not opened separately) [os11, osLT, opened].
explanations: Base-ten blocks/cubes: ones cube, ten rod/tower, hundred flat (IM G1-G2, OpenStax).
Base-ten diagrams drawn from blocks (IM G1 U4 L5, G2 U5 L1).
Ten-frames and connecting-cube towers of ten plus singles (IM G1).
Money $1 $10 $100 bills (OpenStax 1.1).
Place-value chart with periods (OpenStax 1.1); number path 1-99 showing ones digit cycling 0-9 while tens digit steps up (IM G1 L10).
Expanded form 100 + 30 + 8; word form with place names; '8 tens 16 ones' unit form (IM G2 U5 L1).
Number line for rounding and estimating (OpenStax; England Y2).
conventions: English periods of three digits separated by commas (5,278,194) and names thousand, million, billion [os11]. Korean (and Sino-Korean) groups by 10^4: 만, 억, 조 and reads 12,345,678 as 1234만 5678 [korNum]. Korean place names 일 십 백 천 for ones to thousands [kor15, 2015 curriculum quote]. Sino-Korean number words show place value transparently (이십일 = 2-ten-1) unlike English twenty-one/eleven/twelve [korNum; comparison is inference].
'Do not use and' when naming whole numbers in OpenStax; British usage often says 'one hundred and five' - not from an opened source (unverified).
Expanded form, 'standard form' (CC says standard digits) vs UK 'standard form' meaning scientific notation: unverified.
OpenStax and CC use 'ten times the place to its right' [os11, cc4NBT]. IM G2 uses 'compose a hundred'.
misconceptions: IM G1 L10 synthesis: a student wrote 702 for seventy-two; advise that a two-digit number has two digits, no placeholder zero [im1U4L10].
IM G1 L10: students must attend to the unit in each picture rather than read left to right (tens may be drawn on left or right) [im1U4L10].

Gervasoni et al. 2011: many students read, write and order numbers but cannot interpret quantity; Fuson et al. (1997) conceptions of two-digit numbers incl. incorrect single-digits conception (each digit as ones); Cobb & Wheatley (1988) ten as an indivisible single unit; common midpoint-of-0-100 error 10; difficulty with ten less [gervasoni, opened].
NCETM audit: confusing teen numbers such as 13 and 30 [ncetmAudit].
IM G2 U5 L1 notes: watch whether students see 100 as a single unit and can show 100 without ones [im2U5L1].
tasks: Write the number for 3 tens 5 ones; draw 47; 8 tens 16 ones is 96; make the same number with fewer blocks (regrouping); 10 tens = 100.
Name digit values (value of 7 in 573); expanded form; read/write numbers in words.
10 more/10 less; compare using place value; round to nearest 10/100 using number line.

Facts later concepts need: ten of a unit make one of the next unit (base 10), digit value = digit x place value, regrouping for addition/subtraction algorithms, decimals extend to the right; links to [[digits-bases]] (existing page).

curriculum: CC 2.MD.B.6 represent whole numbers as lengths from 0 on a number line diagram with equally spaced points labeled 0, 1, 2, ...; represent sums and differences within 100 on a number line; 2.MD.B.5 ruler-like sketches for length stories [cc2MD, opened]. Brief 2.MD.B.6 correct.

England PoS Y1: use number lines to show numbers and 'more than, less than'; Y2: represent and estimate numbers using different representations including the number line; Y4: count backwards through zero to negatives [eng, opened]. Brief 'Y1-Y6 used throughout' is roughly right but explicit mentions seen only Y1, Y2.
Korean: NOT opened; brief gives no Korean ref for number line (unverified).
textbooks: IM G2 U4 'Addition and Subtraction on the Number Line': A Structure of the Number Line (distances from 0, locate, compare, estimate within 100), B Add and Subtract on a Number Line (arrows and jumps) [im2, opened].

IM G2 U4 L1 'Whole Numbers on the Number Line': compare number line with ruler; fill missing labels on 0-10 line; build own 0-20 line from a strip using a chosen unit (paper clips, base-ten blocks); mark 3 and 13; numbers are distances from 0, evenly spaced; different unit sizes valid; teacher note: check spacing with the unit object [im2U4L1, opened].
IM G2 U5 B and U7 A use number lines to compare and add [im2, opened].

OpenStax Prealgebra 1.1: number line with zero as origin, equally spaced labelled points, numbers increase to the right, a number paired with a point is its coordinate; used for ordering and rounding [os11, osLT, opened].
explanations: Number line as ruler/length from zero (IM G2 U4 L1).
Number path (numerals in boxes) vs number line (points on a line): IES toolkit uses 'number path' for the sequence of numerals [ies].
Paper strip with unit objects laid end to end (IM G2 U4 L1).
String/rope number line, distances proportional to values (Hilton & Hilton 2018).
Arrows and jumps for adding and subtracting (IM G2 U4 B).
Rounding on a number line (OpenStax 1.1).
Mental number line: adjacent numbers differ by one (Griffin et al. 1994, quoted by Gervasoni).
conventions: Number line vs ruler: IM links them (ruler starts at 0, tick marks are at whole numbers) [im2U4L1]. Number lines are drawn left to right in all opened sources [os11, im2U4L1]; direction conventions elsewhere unverified. 'coordinate' used for the number matched with a point [os11]. UK 'number line' is the same term; 'number track' for squares labeled 1,2,3 is UK early-years usage - not from an opened source (unverified).
misconceptions: Hilton & Hilton 2018: absolute thinking (counting on from the first number ignoring scale), additive trial-and-error strategies, halving errors when start is not zero (midpoint of 2 and 8 taken as 3); advice: string number line, vary start, ask how and why, use interval vocabulary [hilton, opened]. Note: that article does not mention counting marks vs spaces; that misconception is NOT sourced.
Gervasoni 2011: most common error placing midpoint of 0-100 as 10 (counting by ones); mental number line supports early arithmetic [gervasoni].
IM G2 U4 L1: students who space ticks unevenly should check with a unit object; use a ruler to check points [im2U4L1].
tasks: Fill in missing labels on 0-10 line; place a point at 7; build a 0-20 line with paper-clip units; mark 3 and 13.
Compare two numbers by position; estimate where 63 goes on 0-100.
Show 5+3 as jumps; 8-3 as a jump back (IM G2 U4 B).
Facts later concepts need: equal spacing, zero origin, order left to right, distance between points = difference; extends to fractions, negatives, coordinate plane.

curriculum: CC 2.OA.C.3 tell whether a group of up to 20 objects is odd or even (pair objects or count by 2s); write an equation expressing an even number as a sum of two equal addends; 2.OA.C.4 arrays up to 5x5 as repeated addition [cc2OA, opened]. Brief 2.OA.C.3 correct. Also 3.OA.D.9: justify that a multiple of 4 is even by splitting into two equal groups [cc3OA, opened].
England PoS Y2: only mention found is 'recognise odd and even numbers' within Y2 multiplication and division (2, 5, 10 tables). Y1 has no such statement [eng, opened].

Korean: per a paper on textbooks, no Korean curriculum lists odd/even as an achievement standard; the 2022 revision adds a note in number and operations (grade 1-2) to treat odd/even within 20 intuitively by pairing objects in real-life contexts; textbook placement moved from Grade 2 (3rd curriculum) to Grade 5 to Grade 1 (2009 and 2015 curricula) [korOE, opened (secondary source)]. 2022 text itself NOT opened.
textbooks: IM G2 U8 'Equal Groups' A Odd and Even (L1 Can You Share?, ..., L3 Is it Odd or Even?), B Rectangular Arrays [im2, opened].

L1: share counters between two so each gets same; table of total/each/leftover; t-chart 'Two Equal Groups' with 'no leftovers' / 'some leftovers'; leftover never more than one; Andre's 17 marbles = 8+8+1 [im2U8L1, opened].

L3: choral count by 2s to 40; color designs with equal yellow and blue; card sort even/odd; find three cards with same number showing even/odd in different ways; accepts pairs, equal groups, counting by 2 [im2U8L3, opened].

NRICH 'add two odd numbers' (ages 5-7) task: dominoes, Multilink cubes in two rows, coloured squares; conjecturing about the sum and explaining why it works for any two odd numbers [nrich8059, opened].
explanations: Pairs / one-to-one matching of objects; a leftover means odd (IM G2 U8, Korean 2009/2015 textbooks).
Two equal groups with or without a leftover (IM G2 U8 L1).
Skip-counting by 2s lands on even numbers (IM L3; CC 2.OA.C.3).
Equation as sum of two equal addends: 12 = 6 + 6 (CC 2.OA.C.3).
Two-row cube/ten-frame arrangement (IM L1 supports); dot patterns with or without a middle dot (IM L3).
Number chart with multiples of 2 marked and ones-digit rule 0,2,4,6,8 (older Korean textbooks; Yuga Crew letter) [korOE, korYuga].
Number line alternation: odd, even, odd, even (korYuga; 4.OA.C.5 notes alternation when adding 3).
conventions: Korean terms 홀수 (odd), 짝수 (even); Korean definitions: 'can be paired in twos' / 'cannot be paired' (2009/2015 textbooks) or multiples of 2; dictionary definition via remainder after dividing by 2 [korOE, korYuga]. English: 'even'/'odd'; IM calls the leftover 'leftovers', CC speaks of 'pairing' [im2U8L1, cc2OA]. Whether 0 is even is treated explicitly only in Korean sources [korOE, korYuga]; English opened pages do not discuss 0 (unverified).
The 짝 (pair/partner) in 짝수 matches the pairing explanation; 홀 (single/lone) - etymology is NOT from an opened source (unverified).
misconceptions: Zero: some students disagree whether 0 is even (alternating pattern vs split into two equal groups) [korOE, opened]. Parent guide: 0 is even because 0 divided by 2 leaves 0 [korYuga].
Justifying sums: in one study of 170 third graders only ~5% justified odd+odd+odd=odd by pairs; ~21% relied on one example [korOE, secondary report].
Korean paper argues first/second graders lack division and remainder language, so 'cannot be paired in twos' as a definition of odd can be unclear [korOE].
IM G2 U8 L1 note: 6 and 7 can both be shown as 2 groups of 3; use to discuss why only one leftover is possible [im2U8L1]. L3: accept any valid method [im2U8L3].
NRICH: use questions 'what do you notice about the answer' and 'can you use your one example to prove it will happen every time' [nrich8059].
tasks: Pair counters/cubes and state odd or even for up to 20; sort cards; count by 2s.
Write an even number as a sum of two equal addends; show odd as double plus 1 (8+8+1=17).
Is a number with ones digit 3 odd? Check numbers beyond 20.
Sum facts: even+even=even, odd+odd=even, even+odd=odd [korYuga; NRICH conjecture task]; 3.OA.D.9 multiples of 4 are even.
Facts later concepts need: 2 divides evenly; parity alternates on number line and in skip-count by 1; link to multiplication by 2 and multiples (2.OA.C.3 -> 3.OA.D.9).

curriculum: CC 2.NBT.A.2 skip-count by 5s, 10s, 100s within 1000; 2.OA.C.3 odd/even via counting by 2s; 3.OA.D.9 identify arithmetic patterns (addition and multiplication tables) and explain using properties; 4.OA.C.5 generate a number or shape pattern from a rule and spot features the rule does not state (start 1 add 3 alternates odd/even); 5.OA.B.3 two patterns from two rules, compare terms, plot as ordered pairs [cc2NBT, cc2OA, cc3OA, cc4OA, cc5OA, opened]. Brief codes correct.

England PoS: Y1 count in 2s, 5s, 10s; Y2 count in 2s, 3s, 5s and tens, and 'order and arrange combinations of mathematical objects in patterns and sequences' (listed under Geometry - position and direction); Y3 count in multiples of 4, 8, 50, 100; Y4 multiples of 6, 7, 9, 25, 1000 [eng, opened]. Y6 and KS3 linear sequences, GCSE A23-A25 NOT opened.

Korean 2022 curriculum text NOT opened: the vivasam/koreascience PDFs returned binary data. Korean codes in brief.json are unverified and may be 2015 or 2022 codes; two 2015-curriculum codes were seen quoted in a paper: [2수01-01] understand numbers 0-100, count/read/write them; [2수01-02] understand 일/십/백/천 place values and positional notation, read/write up to four-digit numbers (source kor15). Brief's [2수02-01..02] for patterns cannot be confirmed.
textbooks: IM G4 U6 A Features of Patterns: L1 'Patterns that Grow' - dot arrays with rows added each step, Han's bottle-cap pattern (several valid rules from two terms), Jada's giraffe pattern (2 squares added per step, predict step 10, can 25 appear?), Andre's house pattern cool-down; representations: diagrams, tables, words, skip-counting, expressions [im4, im4U6L1, opened].
IM G5 U7 C Numerical Patterns: two rules, ordered pairs on a coordinate grid [im5, opened].

IM G2 U8 L3 choral count by 2 to 40 and look for patterns; G2 U5 L1 choral count 90-120; G1 U4 L10 number path 1-99 pattern of ones and tens digits [im2U8L3, im2U5L1, im1U4L10, opened]. IM G4 U1 B patterns in factors and multiples [im4].
explanations: Repeating patterns of objects first, then growing patterns (AAMT Top Drawer).
Skip counting with number line or hundred chart; choral count recorded on chart (IM).
Shape/dot growth patterns by step number; tables of step vs total (IM G4 U6 L1).
Rule in words, as repeated addition, as multiplication expression (IM G4 U6 L1).
Position-to-term rule vs term-to-term rule (AAMT: successive-term rules or linking position to value).
Two sequences plotted on coordinate plane (IM G5 U7 C; CC 5.OA.B.3).
conventions: Terminology: 'pattern' (CC, IM) vs 'sequence' (England Y2 'patterns and sequences', AAMT 'number sequences'); 'rule' (CC 4.OA.C.5, IM); England 'counting in steps/multiples of' vs US 'skip counting' [eng, cc2NBT, cc4OA, topdrawer]. Both repeating (fixed unit of repeat) and growing patterns [topdrawer]. Korean 규칙 (rule/pattern) term: unverified, not from an opened page.
misconceptions: AAMT Top Drawer: repeating patterns have a fixed unit of repeat but growing patterns do not; students often find rules hard to identify; rules can be term-to-term or position-to-value; start with repeating patterns, concrete then pictures then abstract [topdrawer, opened].

IM G4 U6 L1: with only two steps shown, several rules fit (add 5, double, increase the increase); constant change vs constant multiplier vs changing change; students notice alternating odd/even, multiples of 5/10; checking whether a number (25, 72) can appear reinforces the rule [im4U6L1].
CC 4.OA.C.5: sequence from 1 adding 3 alternates odd and even and students should explain why [cc4OA].
No research citation on skip-counting errors was found in opened pages (unverified).
tasks: Continue a repeating pattern (AB, ABB); continue skip counts by 2, 5, 10; find the missing number in a sequence.
Describe the rule; state the next three terms; will 25 appear? (IM G4).
Growing dot patterns: count for steps 1-6 in a table; predict step 10.
Sequence from rule 'start 1, add 3' and its odd/even alternation; two sequences with rules add 3 and add 6 from 0 (second is double the first, CC 5.OA.B.3).
Facts later concepts need: skip counts give multiplication tables (2.NBT.A.2 -> multiplication), term-to-term rule is recursion, position-to-value rule is a function/linear relation.
